tagline: Rainforest islands of the western Pacific
overview:
Solomon Islands is a scattered nation of roughly 1,000 islands in Melanesia, southeast of Papua New Guinea and northeast of Australia. Six main islands, including Guadalcanal, Malaita and Santa Isabel, hold most of the land, which totals about 28,900 km², a little smaller than Belgium, spread across a great expanse of ocean.

About 800,000 people live here. English is the official language, but almost everyone speaks Solomon Islands Pijin as a common tongue, and more than 60 local languages are spoken at home. Honiara, on Guadalcanal, is the capital.

Solomon Islands is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. Most families live in villages, growing sweet potato, taro and cassava and fishing the lagoons; logging, fish and palm oil are the main exports. The islands are known for rainforest, spectacular diving over World War II wrecks, and shell money still used in traditional exchanges.
landAndNature: The islands are mostly volcanic, with steep forested interiors, rivers and narrow coastal flats; Mount Popomanaseu on Guadalcanal reaches about 2,335 meters. Kavachi, an underwater volcano in the west, erupts often and has sharks living inside its crater. Marovo Lagoon is one of the largest saltwater lagoons in the world, enclosed by a double barrier reef. The forests hold cuscus, a slow-moving marsupial, huge monitor lizards, and hornbills, while the reefs are part of the Coral Triangle, with hundreds of coral species. The Solomons is home to the world's largest extinct-volcano atoll, and its beaches host leatherback turtles. Cyclones and earthquakes strike regularly; a tsunami in 2007 destroyed coastal villages.
peopleAndCulture: Most Solomon Islanders are Melanesian, with Polynesian communities on some outer islands and Micronesian settlers on others. Wealth and ceremony can still involve shell money: strings of tiny shell discs, cut, drilled and polished mainly on Malaita, are used for bride-price and compensation. Panpipe orchestras from Malaita play interlocking bamboo melodies, and bamboo bands beat lengths of pipe with rubber sandals to make deep booming notes. Food is cooked in stone ovens, and fish with taro or cassava pudding is common. Canoes carved from a single log, some with inlaid shell decoration, remain important for travel and fishing. Soccer and futsal are popular, and the national futsal team has done well in Oceania.
history: People settled these islands at least 30,000 years ago, and Austronesian voyagers arrived later, bringing pottery and new crops. Spanish navigator Álvaro de Mendaña reached them in 1568 and named them after the biblical King Solomon, hoping for gold that was never found. In the 1800s blackbirding ships carried thousands of islanders, sometimes by force or trickery, to work on plantations in Queensland and Fiji. Britain declared a protectorate in 1893. During World War II the Battle of Guadalcanal, from August 1942 to February 1943, was a turning point in the Pacific, and the seabed off Honiara, nicknamed Iron Bottom Sound, holds dozens of sunken ships. Independence came on July 7, 1978. Ethnic conflict between 1998 and 2003 was ended with the help of a regional peacekeeping mission.
funFacts: Around one in ten Solomon Islanders has naturally blond hair with dark skin, caused by a gene found almost nowhere else.
Strings of polished shell discs are still used as money for bride-price and settling disputes.
The waters off Honiara are called Iron Bottom Sound because so many warships sank there during World War II.
Sharks have been filmed living inside the crater of Kavachi, an active undersea volcano, between eruptions.
A young John F. Kennedy was rescued here in 1943 after islanders carried his message carved on a coconut shell.
